title: Jason Arday: Ex-Cambridge professor cancels live event after plagiarism row
description: In another development, BBC News has learned that Arday resigned on Sunday as a publication director and trustee of the British Sociological Associati
body: In another development, BBC News has learned that Arday resigned on Sunday as a publication director and trustee of the British Sociological Association (BSA), the national body for sociology academics.The BSA, to which Arday gave a lecture earlier this year claiming black academics were being targeted in "evil" ways, told the BBC it would shortly amend its website to reflect the change.It was one of multiple roles Arday held in various organisations.The NHS Race and Health Observatory - which studies racial and ethnic inequality in health - lists him as a member of its "academic reference advisory group", citing his now-out-of-date Cambridge title. Arday was also named as a fellow of the Royal Society of Arts by Cambridge when it appointed him.Neither organisation replied to the BBC's request for clarification on whether they remained current roles.Arday also sat on ITV's Cultural Advisory Council and as an expert the Welsh Government's anti-racism external accountability group, but both roles ended earlier this year.When asked by the BBC, Advance HE declined to confirm whether Arday remains a senior fellow of its formerly named Higher Education Academy, citing data protection law. The senior fellowship is awarded to individuals who "lead or influence the learning and teaching practices of others".The Runnymede Trust think tank, for whom Arday was a trustee until 2024, released a statement defending him last week and condemning "racialised, hyper-aggressive media scrutiny".The publisher of Arday's memoir Great and Unfortunate Things is going ahead with its release in the US on Tuesday and in the UK on 27 August as planned.The book tells the story of his life from being non-verbal until the age of 11 and unable to read or write until 18, then going through a series of "improbable triumphs and heartbreaking setbacks", before being appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge.However, he has been accused of plagiarism in his PhD thesis, and questions have been raised about the reliability of parts of his life story, including that he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5m for charity.On Wednesday, the University of Cambridge said it had launched an investigation "following new information" about his "academic qualifications and honorary appointments".Announcing his resignation on the same day, Arday said the "personal cost" of the scrutiny had become "too great".He said: "While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement."The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."He stressed that his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

schema.headline: Jason Arday: Ex-Cambridge professor cancels live event after plagiarism row

title: Jeff Bezos & Liverpool: Consortium including American advances talks
description: A consortium including billionaire Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has advanced its talks to buy about a 30% stake in Liverpool, BBC Sport has been told.The
body: A consortium including billionaire Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has advanced its talks to buy about a 30% stake in Liverpool, BBC Sport has been told.The group is led by British-Indian millionaire businessman Amit Bhatia and also includes Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin.Owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG) confirmed last month that the group had "expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club".Bhatia is the son-in-law of Indian billionaire businessman Lakshmi Mittal and had been a director and co-owner of Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before relinquishing his stake in the club last month.American businessman Bezos, founder of e-commerce giant Amazon, is the fourth-richest person in the world.According to Forbes, the 62-year-old has an estimated net worth of $256bn (£192bn).FSG, who bought Liverpool in a £300m deal in 2010, previously sold a minority stake in the Anfield side to global sports investment firm Dynasty Equity. BBC Sport contacted FSG about the latest developments, but they had no further comment.In January, Liverpool became the top-earning Premier League club for the first time, according to analysis from financial firm Deloitte. The following month the club announced record revenues of £703m for 2024-25 financial year.

schema.headline: Jeff Bezos & Liverpool: Consortium including American advances talks

title: MSP apologises over controversial rape 'demonisation' comments
description: The comments have been widely criticised by survivors groups and political opponents who said they downplayed the seriousness and lasting trauma of ra
body: The comments have been widely criticised by survivors groups and political opponents who said they downplayed the seriousness and lasting trauma of rape.The SCRA, which comprises support groups in Glasgow, Lanarkshire, Ayrshire and the Western Isles, said the impacts of rape can last a lifetime, and the crime should never be reduced to a theoretical debate. In an open letter the alliance said: "We are not demonising rape. We are naming it."The authors strongly opposed the idea of rape existing on a "spectrum", insisting "there is no hierarchy of rape" and that no survivor should feel compelled to ask whether their experience was serious enough."The letter urged politicians "not to normalise" rape or sexual violence, and "not create hierarchies of harm". While not naming Manivannan, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on Violence against Women and Girls, Reem Alsalem, posted on X that rape should never be spoken about in terms of it being a spectrum.Scotland's Children's Minister Siobhan Brown told the BBC's Sunday Show Manivannan's words were misjudged. Scottish Labour and the Scottish Liberal Democrats have also been critical, while the Scottish Conservatives called on the Scottish Greens to suspend the MSP.Meghan Gallacher, the party's equalities spokeswoman, said: "It is deeply alarming that anyone, but especially an elected representative, would ever seek to minimise the seriousness of rape and suggest that there is a spectrum of offences."In a statement issued on Monday afternoon, Manivannan said they were "horrified" that the comments had been "selectively edited in order to mislead people and misrepresent me". The MSP said that during the interview they had categorically stated that every rape in every context is equally serious and harmful but this had been "maliciously" left out of clips. They added: "I recognise that the words in the clip shared, without the full context of the conversation, have caused considerable upset. "For that I apologise. I will always stand with and for victims and survivors."Manivannan said they were themselves a survivor of sexual violence and understood the enduring trauma of such an experience. "I would never seek to diminish or dismiss any survivor's experience, or to make anyone feel that their pain was not heard or understood," they added. "I am genuinely sorry to everyone who has been distressed, hurt or triggered by the clips, and by the discussion and coverage that has followed. "Words matter, particularly when speaking about something as deeply personal and painful as sexual violence, and I regret this hurt caused."

schema.headline: MSP apologises over controversial rape 'demonisation' comments

title: We should smile at our dogs - a new scientific study reveals why
description: Image source, Laura CuayaImage caption, Kun-kun, a very good dog, sits patiently in the brain scanner ByVictoria GillScience correspondentAny dog love
body: Image source, Laura CuayaImage caption, Kun-kun, a very good dog, sits patiently in the brain scanner ByVictoria GillScience correspondentAny dog lover will tell you their canine friend picks up on their mood and emotions.Now scientists have worked out exactly what is going on inside a dog's brain when it sees a human - even a complete stranger - smiling or scowling.Their research involved 14 dogs in total who all sat very still in a brain scanner while they were shown pictures of people's faces.Photographs of happy, smiling human faces made an area of the brain that is associated with reward "light up" with activity.This reward circuitry is the part of the brain that is activated when we enjoy and remember good things, like tasty food or praise.In terms of our own  brains, we often refer to it as the "dopamine hit" that is triggered  by winning a game or even receiving a positive comment on a social media post.Image source, Eniko KubinyiImage caption, The dogs were shown images of strangers' faces with different expressionsIn previous research on dogs, the same brain region has been found to light up when the dogs anticipated a tasty snack, or smelled a familiar person."It controls us having motivation to do things - wanting to do things," explained Laura Cuaya, one of the study's lead researchers at the University of Vienna. "So this finding suggests that happy faces, even those of strangers have a positive value for dogs."Cuaya and her co-researcher, Raúl Hernández-Pérez, went on to investigate how dogs responded to other human emotions - showing dogs images of people displaying happiness, anger, fear, and sadness. But the reward circuitry only responded to happy faces."Dogs can distinguish between positive emotions and all the others, but they don't seem to be able to distinguish between the different negative emotions," Hernández-Pérez, also at the University of Vienna, told BBC News.Image source, Laura Cuaya/University of ViennaImage caption, Researchers Raúl Hernández-Pérez and Laura Cuaya with their dogs Odín and Kun-kun Laura Cuaya and Raúl Hernández-Pérez are partners in research and in life - and something of a canine-cognition power couple. After meeting at secondary school in Mexico the two went on to work together on research projects that have revealed how dogs interpret and respond to human language and behaviour.It is work that has revealed insights into the biology underlying the unique relationship between humans and their dogs.The couple's own border collies, Odín and Kun-kun, have taken part in several of their research projects - including this one. And the couple recruited other dogs - and their owners - for their studies by politely approaching people in the dog park."If we saw someone with a dog that was the right size [for the scanner] - and looked calm and like it was well trained, we'd ask if they would be interested in helping," recalled Hernández-Pérez.How humans changed dogs' brainsImage source, Laura CuayaImage caption, Odín and Kun-kun examine their own brain scans Cuaya explained that, from a neuroscience perspective, "the dog's brain is quite fascinating"."They are really good at understanding emotions in humans - a species that is completely different from them."This research is building a picture of exactly how thousands of years of living alongside humans has made this possible by moulding and changing dogs' brain circuitry."When we compare humans with other primates, we are looking at abilities that may have come from a common ancestor," Cuaya added."With dogs, the story is totally different. They followed a very different evolutionary path, but through domestication, they developed the social abilities needed to understand and cooperate with us."Cuaya and Hernández-Pérez also hope their findings will help show people to communicate more effectively with their own beloved canine companions."We can reward our dogs with treats, but also reward them with happiness," said Cuaya. "So we should smile at the dogs - even at random dogs in the street."The findings are published in the journal iScience, external.

schema.headline: We should smile at our dogs - a new scientific study reveals why

title: UK heatwaves: Satellite images show impact of hot, dry summer
description: From Stonehenge to the Serpentine - satellite images show impact of hot, dry summerByRob CorpBarbara Metzler and Thomas SpencerBBC VerifyWith more par
body: From Stonehenge to the Serpentine - satellite images show impact of hot, dry summerByRob CorpBarbara Metzler and Thomas SpencerBBC VerifyWith more parts of England set to join Wales as being officially declared to be in drought, BBC Verify has been gathering satellite imagery showing the impact of this year's extreme summer heat.From historic sites and parks to reservoirs and golf courses, the hot, dry weather has changed how large parts of the UK usually look.This year's consecutive heatwaves and above-average temperatures have had a noticeable effect -  even compared with last summer which was the UK's warmest on record.Drop in Welsh reservoir levelAccording to the UK government, almost all reservoirs in England and Wales are officially classed as having water levels below normal or low.Five are exceptionally low - among them Clywedog reservoir in Powys which provides water supplies for parts of the West Midlands.These satellite images show how more of the banks of the reservoir are visible this August compared with the same month last year.Low reservoir levels have not been the primary cause of recent hosepipe bans and drought declarations - which are ultimately triggered by a lack of rain - across large parts of England and Wales.The Environment Agency has reported that reservoir storage is now at 69% in England, which is below the long-term average of 82% for the time of year but higher than during last year's drought.However, in its latest report the agency says water storage levels are above those recorded during similar periods in 2022 and 2025.While Scotland has not been as badly affected as England and Wales, July's rainfall was below average for the south and east of the country, with many areas seeing less than half the long-term average for the month.This has led the Scottish Environment Protection Agency to warn of "significant" water scarcity in the Borders and "moderate scarcity" in areas on the eastern side of Scotland.Brown fairways at Open golf courseHard and dry fairways were a key talking point at golf's Open Championship which was held at Royal Birkdale on Merseyside last month.A side-by-side comparison shows how much greener the fairways appeared in summer 2025 compared with this year.As the BBC reported earlier this month while domestic users face hosepipe restrictions the rules for commercial users - including golf courses - vary.When hosepipe bans are in force sports grounds can use hoses or sprinklers - but only to water grass areas "actively used for play". For golf courses this means the greens and tees can be irrigated but the fairways cannot.Algal blooms in reservoirs and lakesRight in the heart of the UK capital, Hyde Park's famous Serpentine lake was closed for swimming on Monday because of high levels of blue-green algae.Blue-green algae occur naturally, but warm, sunny and settled conditions can help blooms develop. Some can be harmful to people and animals.A similar issue is affecting Killington Reservoir in south Cumbria. Satellite images show a visible change in the water between 24 May and 8 August, where a blue-green algal bloom has been confirmed.Looking at the rest of Hyde Park and what is one of London's prime green spaces is now mostly brown following consecutive heatwaves since May.It's a similar sight in south Wiltshire where the usually green rolling fields surrounding the ancient stone circle at Stonehenge have become almost as pale as the path around the prehistoric site.As BBC Verify previously reported parts of the country are suffering from "vegetation stress" where the development and growth of plants, grass and crops can be severely affected.Vegetation turning brown, even on this scale, does not mean the plants have disappeared or died, as grass, shrubs and some trees can recover once rainfall returns, provided their root systems remain intact.Experts have said the combination of next-to-no rainfall and prolonged hot weather is likely to cause significant issues for the farming industry and could have an impact on agriculture and food prices in the coming months.And perhaps counter-intuitively, prolonged dry weather can raise the risk of flash flooding when it eventually does rain. That is because parched, rock-hard ground may struggle to absorb water at first, so some rainwater may simply run off the surface instead.Scientists also warn the UK is facing a growing risk of water shortages in the decades ahead, driven by human-caused climate change and increased demand.Graphics by Tom Shiel

schema.headline: UK heatwaves: Satellite images show impact of hot, dry summer

title: Derby County investment: Deal off as Turki Alalshikh shelves plans
description: Saudi Arabia government official Turki Alalshikh has abandoned his proposed investment into Derby County.The deal with Alalshikh's Lion Sport looked s
body: Saudi Arabia government official Turki Alalshikh has abandoned his proposed investment into Derby County.The deal with Alalshikh's Lion Sport looked set to go ahead, having been sanctioned by the English Football League (EFL) and the Independent Football Regulator (IFR).But Derby were told on Monday that Alalshikh no longer wanted to continue with the purchase of his stake."For the benefit of any doubt, the club is now off the market," a club statement said."It will continue to operate under the loyal, committed and unwavering support of Clowes Developments."In a statement on social media, Alalshikh thanked those at Derby County for their involvement in the proposed deal, but suggested the time it took to be ratified meant he had to withdraw."We understood that the IFR process takes time and fully respect the importance of that," he posted on X. "But unfortunately with the season already started, it would leave us with no time to prepare the team or the club for the season ahead. "After careful consideration, we don't feel it is right to proceed at this time without the necessary preparation in place, but we will remain in conversation with the club and see what is possible in the future."A deal for Alalshikh, the co-founder of boxing promotion company Zuffa, to take a stake in the Championship club had been on the table with the football regulator since May.An IFR spokesperson said: "The IFR has a statutory duty to thoroughly test all prospective owners of a club in the top five divisions of men's football."The assessment was completed in 55 days out of the 90 days allowed by law. "The IFR had taken a 'minded-to decision' to approve the bid before the start of the 2026-27 season. This had been communicated to all parties last week."In every case, we must consider a broad but fixed list of matters, all set out in statute. "This includes assessing all candidates against the IFR's test on financial soundness, sufficient financial resources, source of wealth, and honesty and integrity - including a check on any criminal proceedings or convictions, civil actions and other regulatory investigations."The proposed deal had raised concerns among human rights campaigners, including Amnesty International, which said in June that the independent regulator faced a "defining test" over the investment.Alalshikh, the chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority - and someone who is close to the Kingdom's de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman - has been criticised by human rights groups for his role in alleged 'sportswashing'.Saudi Arabia has been accused of using sports to improve its image in the wider world to distract from its human rights record, treatment of women, use of the death penalty and its anti-LGBT stance.As well as being the owner of Egyptian club Pyramids between 2018 and 2019, Alalshikh recently owned Spanish side Almeria but sold the club to an investment group from Saudi Arabia last May.

schema.headline: Derby County investment: Deal off as Turki Alalshikh shelves plans

title: European Athletics Championships: New guidelines for more respectful TV camera coverage of female athletes used for first time
description: New guidelines for broadcasters on using more respectful camera angles when covering live athletics events have been implemented for the first time at
body: New guidelines for broadcasters on using more respectful camera angles when covering live athletics events have been implemented for the first time at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham.The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) developed the guidelines following discussions with female athletes to avoid sexualising the sporting action with unnecessary camera angles.The first European Athletics Championships to be held in Great Britain got under way at Alexander Stadium on Monday morning.British pole vaulter Molly Caudery, a two-time world indoor champion, told BBC Newsbeat: "It's not controversial, it's a very sensible decision. It is a positive guidance and change."I have experienced it. For this to change for up-and-coming athletes is such a positive change. "In pole vault, there are so many angles you can film from, so just taking one out is not going to be an issue. "It will hopefully lead to everyone just focusing on performance."The guidelines, released last month, give advice on how broadcasters should use more respectful camera angles when covering live athletics events.The rules were created in consultation with athletes including former British pole vaulter Holly Bradshaw, Serbian long jumper Ivana Spanovic, and Croatian high jumper Blanka Vlasic.It details 'positive' and 'negative' angles that could arise in various sporting scenarios. Things to avoid include low camera angles underneath athletes in events such as the high jump or pole vault, which have a high chance of generating compromising images. Former middle-distance athlete Hannah England, who was involved in developing the guidelines, said: "To be blunt, if you go on the internet and search certain athletes, you get bombarded with clips of them competing in compromising positions. That's just not OK."On the implementation of the guidance, England added: "It is hard to broadcast athletics. You could be on a safe shot of an athlete and they then need to tie their shoe or pick up a piece of equipment, and you can't anticipate that."You can't hold people to a super-high standard in an environment that's impossible to police, so I think guidelines are 100% the way to go."British Olympic bronze medallist Bradshaw was among the athletes to advise the EBU. The pole vaulter says she has been sent abuse on social media and has seen inappropriate videos of herself online because of revealing camera angles during live coverage of her competitions."How our sport is displayed during live broadcast can be incredibly powerful, yet sometimes harmful to the women competing and the women [and] girls watching," she said."I first-hand have received social media abuse and witnessed inappropriate videos online of myself and colleagues when slow-motion content of us competing is captured."Many athletes, myself included have been in competitive scenarios where they are more focused on the cameras instead of their own performance.  "On too many occasions cameras are zoomed in, showing super slow-motion action replays of athletes in undignified positions."Serbian Olympic long jumper Spanovic, who also gave advice to the EBU, said certain cameras not only cause discomfort during events but can have "serious long-term effects on an athlete's mental health".EBU Sport executive director Glen Killane said: "The sexualisation of women athletes through selective camera angles and editing choices continues to be a significant concern across many sports broadcasts."Lingering shots on bodies, low-angle cameras that capture revealing views, and excessive slow-motion replays that serve no technical or storytelling purpose are among the issues observed in the media coverage of women's athletics competitions today."The BBC is a partner in the EBU, which provides coverage of sporting events to 57 countries, reaching audiences of more than a billion people.   While the new guidance has been implemented at the European Athletics Championships, the Diamond League - which is also broadcast on the BBC - does not go through the EBU and so would not necessarily have to adhere to the guidance.

schema.headline: European Athletics Championships: New guidelines for more respectful TV camera coverage of female athletes used for first time

title: Tech leaders say AI means less work - their staff say they work up to 90 hours a week
description: For years now, executives at companies that are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars a year into developing various artificial intelligence tools h
body: For years now, executives at companies that are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars a year into developing various artificial intelligence tools have insisted that the technology will ultimately mean people will spend less of their time working.An engineering director at Google said four years ago that AI would deliver a four-day work week by 2025, external.Earlier this year, and just one year after that engineering director's prediction, OpenAI took up the challenge, in a manner of speaking. It formally urged companies to start testing out a four-day work week (with no change in pay), claiming that AI will soon be able to speed up so much human labour that the corporate world should prepare itself.However, a former OpenAI technical employee who left the company last year told the BBC the firm never actually trialled the four-day work week it suggested others should try while they were there.Instead, the person described what was often a gruelling work culture marked by frequent "crisis meetings", working on weekends, and "super cut-throat" performance reviews that would see colleagues suddenly let go."You go in on Saturday or Sunday just to catch up or make sure things aren't broken," the person said.Other companies have also pushed the idea that AI will effectively reduce the number of hours people need to work, for better or worse.Anthropic has boasted that its popular coding tool and chatbot Claude is capable of working on its own for seven hours without a break, external, essentially a full corporate workday. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg has said his company is in the middle of the year when "AI starts to dramatically change the way that we work" and that such tools let far fewer employees do more than they ever could have before.While Meta has since laid off 1 in 10 of its employees, Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei has warned that as AI tools inevitably become more productive, it could mean, external even broader job losses.Despite these claims, workers inside these same tech companies, who are not only developing but using the very AI tools that will purportedly perform at least some of people's work, say they are clocking in far more than the typical five-day, 40-hour work week.US tech workers are typically well-compensated, external, and while other industries such as investment banking, law and medicine also often see people work long hours, a 14-hour workday was not always the norm in tech. For years, it was a more typical 9-5 office job.But the former OpenAI employee said they would put in at least 70 hours a week, much more than they did in previous tech jobs. The person now works at a start-up also focused on AI, and said their work-life balance has improved, working closer to 50-60 hours a week, "outside of sprints".A "sprint" is term for a common period in technology companies in which people work long hours in the weeks leading up to a release of a new feature or product.Inside AI companies and larger tech companies working furiously on AI projects, however, such sprints can be extreme. At OpenAI and Anthropic, for instance, sprints can stretch on for many weeks and top 90 hours of work in a seven-day period, tech workers that the BBC spoke to for this story said.Neither company responded to BBC requests for comment. At Meta, workers said they have been abruptly pushed onto teams this year doing AI work being treated as urgent. They called it being "drafted", according to one current and one former employee, because people were not given a choice."They just move you over," the former employee said. "You can't say no – or if you do, you have to quit."They said although Meta recently began to walk back, external that strict take it or leave us approach, by then many workers had already been forced onto such work.The hours on such teams at Meta are often long, with staff working into the night, on weekends, and feeling they are "on call" during the hours they are not working, according to descriptions of the work from the current and former employees.There are no limits, external in the US on how many hours a person over the age of 16 can work. In the UK and Europe, for instance, laws limit a working week to 48 hours, including overtime.Meta's current AI projects include the creation of an AI tool that can be used for software engineering and other kinds of work, and building AI model infrastructure that can measure an AI model's success in replicating various tasks, the employees added."You're literally working in teams of people trying to replicate humans doing jobs," the former employee said.That work, the person added, seems "endless".A Meta spokesperson declined to comment.Even tech workers who are not directly involved in the development of AI tools are facing longer hours due to the technology.A former Google employee, Amin Shali, left the company in May due to the ways in which he claimed AI was negatively impacting his job, like having to often work all hours of the night because internal engineering functions had failed. This was happening more frequently as Google moved crucial resources like processing units and memory storage over to AI projects.A Google spokesperson declined to comment.Since leaving Google, Shali told the BBC that his sleep and overall health had improved. He said he's realised that heavy reliance on AI tools in large tech companies "creates a bad culture with excess pressure on engineers".Some new research suggests that AI tools are making people's workloads even more burdensome.A study, external out of UC Berkeley followed hundreds of workers at a US tech company for eight months as they used AI. It found the employees "worked at a faster pace, took on a broader scope of tasks, and extended work into more hours of the day".Neil Thompson, an innovation scholar at MIT, said that even at tech companies leading on AI development, it is unlikely that workers are being told to simply deploy the tools that are supposed to do some of their work and move on."It leads to a situation where even if there were real time savings, it would be sucked up by the changes, and implementing them, and making sure they worked," Thompson said.The UC Berkeley research found that the workload of tech employees was expanded in part because of the need to constantly check the output of AI tools.In a situation where an employee had smoothed out processes for AI tools, people also tend to fill any time saved with more work, Thompson added, either because they want to or they feel they should do in order to prove their value to an employer."People assume that 20% less work means four-day weeks," Thompson said. "But new work emerges."As Shali observed: "AI is supposed to be doing so much for us now, so many more people should at least have better health and better sleep."Instead, it seems to be the opposite.

schema.headline: Tech leaders say AI means less work - their staff say they work up to 90 hours a week

title: Benjamin Netanyahu's rejection of Trump's 15-point Gaza plan unlikely to be final word
description: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have categorically rejected the new Board of Peace roadmap to disarm Hamas in Gaza, but that is unlikel
body: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have categorically rejected the new Board of Peace roadmap to disarm Hamas in Gaza, but that is unlikely to be the final word.The White House has not officially commented. However, it is reportedly "not bothered" by Netanyahu's statement and views it as campaign rhetoric in the run-up to a heated general election."We understand Bibi's political needs" the Israeli journalist, Barak Ravid, quotes a senior US official as saying – using a nickname to refer to the Israeli leader. "We have no problem with it as long as he continues to do what we ask – especially regarding restraining attacks in Gaza."Recent days have seen an apparent pause in Israel's strikes on Gaza – something Hamas had demanded when signing on to the US-backed, 15-point roadmap.And there is another suggestion that Israel is ready to advance US President Donald Trump's peace plan for Gaza – getting ready for the deployment of the International Stabilization Force (ISF). The force is made up of international troops, with the plan being for them to work with a new Palestinian police force to secure the territory.The expected construction of the first ISF base is still scheduled to begin amid the ruins of Rafah in southern Gaza at the end of this month, according to Israeli public radio, Kan News, which would allow reconstruction to begin at last.In July, after months of delicate negotiations, Trump announced a "major milestone" in the implementation of his plan to end Israel's war in Gaza. Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump said that the Board of Peace had reached an agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups in the territory.The deal is meant to be carried out in phases, with all weapons decommissioned and stored by a new Palestinian administration in Gaza – which reports to the Board of Peace - and Israeli forces withdrawing from the more than 60% of Gaza they currently control.Senior Hamas officials confirmed that they had agreed to the new framework, conditioning it on mutual compliance by Israel. This was widely viewed as a major potential breakthrough in the conflict. The UK welcomed it and the European Union hailed it as a "crucial step".However, for more than a week, Israel did not give its formal response. An Israeli spokesman said only that the roadmap did not "reflect Israel's positions." A far-right member of the government, Itamar Ben-Gvir, wrote on X that the deal was "unacceptable."Increasingly, mainstream Israeli opposition politicians also raised doubts. They questioned whether all small arms would be decommissioned and the sequencing of the plan.Finally on Sunday, Netanyahu told his cabinet, "I wish to be precise here: Israel does not accept the 15-point document."He added: "The IDF [Israel Defense Forces] will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament."In the same statement, the prime minister described President Trump as "the greatest of our friends in the White House" but said that Israel knew "how to stand firm" against unacceptable ideas.In Israel, there is widespread scepticism that Hamas intends to follow through on its commitments. The Islamist movement has long seen "armed struggle" as a core precept, its legitimate response to Israeli occupation of Palestinian lands. In recent months, there had been signs of it reasserting its authority in Gaza."Israel can certainly never agree to retreating anywhere where the terrorist group that caused the worst massacres since the Holocaust is still there and is still ruling the Strip," Fleur Hassan-Nahoum, an Israeli commentator and former deputy mayor of Jerusalem told the BBC.She stressed that the "trauma of the Israeli people" from the deadly Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023, which ignited the devastating Gaza war, should not be underestimated.Any potential concessions for Netanyahu would come at a politically sensitive moment. He is facing an uphill contest in the upcoming general election, scheduled for 27 October. It will be Israel's first since the 7 October assault and three years on, Netanyahu has failed to secure what he vowed: "absolute victory" over Hamas.The former American diplomat and veteran Middle East negotiator, Aaron David Miller, said the Israeli leader is facing "the most consequential election" of his political life. "He's navigating a very fine line between keeping his constituents happy and not angering or alienating President Trump," he told the BBC.For now, he believes the White House recognises the situation and is giving Netanyahu "a pass."  Miller added: "It's hard to believe that you're going to see any serious movement before you have another Israeli government."In the meantime, the Board of Peace has been trying to reassure the Israeli public about the roadmap.The High Commissioner for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov – who led months of delicate negotiations with Hamas – gave an interview to Israel's Channel 12 just hours after Netanyahu's formal rejection of the roadmap."Its goal is to make sure that Gaza is never again a threat to Israeli security and that what happened before, [on] October 7, never happens again," he said.He said the deal takes "a step-by-step approach" meaning: "If there is verified decommissioning of weapons, that they are taken away from the factions and stored and ultimately rendered unusable, Israel then withdraws from Gaza."Ultimately, Mladenov said that nothing was being built "on the basis of trust" but on "verification."Hamas has since indicated that it still remains committed to the roadmap. It called on mediators and the Board of Peace to push for Israel to stick to the terms agreed.The Israeli prime minister has confirmed that talks with the Americans are continuing.Meanwhile heavy pressure from Washington is likely to increase.Trump is also looking at an important election this year – November's midterm elections for the US Congress. His Republican party faces the prospect of heavy losses, with petrol and grocery prices pushed up, in part due to Washington's unpopular five-month-long war in Iran.The US president's own approval rating has tumbled, and he may well demand positive developments in his peace plan for Gaza in an effort to score a much-needed foreign policy win.

schema.headline: Benjamin Netanyahu's rejection of Trump's 15-point Gaza plan unlikely to be final word

title: World's oceans hit record-high July temperatures
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByJessica RawnsleyThe world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, partly fuelled by developing El
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByJessica RawnsleyThe world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, partly fuelled by developing El Niño conditions in the Pacific, according to the EU's climate monitoring service.The average sea surface temperature (SST) outside the world's polar regions - between 60 degrees north and 60 degrees south - was 20.96C last month, beating the previous high of 20.89C, set in 2023.Last month was the joint second-warmest July globally on record, with temperatures 1.47C above the estimated pre-industrial average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.Meanwhile, Western Europe experienced its hottest ever June and July, with prolonged hot and dry conditions fuelling extreme wildfires across the region.Elsewhere, the UK is braced for its fifth heatwave of the year this week, as persistent dry weather puts further pressure on water supplies and could see more areas officially declared in drought.Around Europe, sea surface temperatures in July reached record highs along the Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean, contributing to widespread strong and severe marine heatwaves.Sea temperatures remained exceptionally high across much of the tropical Pacific, where El Niño conditions are developing and forecast to strengthen in the coming months. El Niño is a natural weather pattern in the Pacific that combined with human-driven global warming can cause temperature spikes and more extreme weather.Oceans are a vital regulator of the climate, absorbing most of the excess heat generated by greenhouse gas emissions and producing half of Earth's oxygen.The greatest effect of ocean warming is on sea level rise. As seawater warms it expands, and this thermal expansion accounts for roughly a third of sea level rise recorded by scientists to date. That water encroaches on low-lying coasts and island nations.Hotter seas are also driving longer and fiercer marine heatwaves, which have bleached coral reefs on a mass scale and decimated kelp forests and fisheries.Warmer ocean surfaces also evaporate more heat and moisture into the air, intensifying tropical storms and loading them with heavier rainfall.'Climate change is intensifying heat extremes'Western Europe is experiencing an exceptional run of extreme heat - with record-breaking temperatures in June and July, and some areas facing their third or fourth heat wave since May.The average temperature across western Europe for June and July was 21.62C - 2.79C above average and the highest for the two-month period."July 2026 was the third consecutive month of exceptional heat in western Europe," said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.Persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over the region, she said, while dry soils reduced the ability to provide natural cooling."This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another," she added.France, Spain, parts of Germany and the UK recorded exceptionally low rainfall and/or soil moisture, while soil moisture levels across much of western Europe were significantly lower than in 2022, when the region experienced severe drought.River levels have been much lower than average - in some places exceptionally low -with the Seine, Rhine and Danube among those particularly affected.Low flows exacerbate pressure on water supplies and irrigation, aquatic ecosystems, river transport and energy production.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Some rivers in Europe have recorded extremely low water levels, including the Danube The prolonged hot and dry conditions have created favourable conditions for wildfires, with massive wildfires raging across western Europe last month and "exceptional activity" in terms of the area burned and smoke and emissions generated."Climate change is increasingly bringing the kinds of hot and dry conditions that favour large, high-intensity wildfires in southern Europe while extended the fire season northwards," said Laurence Rouil, director of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service.Larger fires produce more smoke and inject it higher into the atmosphere, allowing it to travel much further, he said.That means countries that experience relatively few wildfires could be increasingly affected by smoke traveling long distances.Extreme weather 'new normal'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, European wildfires haven been called "completely unprecedented" this summerIn the UK, meanwhile, the prolonged dry spell is increasing pressure on already-stretched water supplies.England and Wales recorded their driest July since records began 190 years ago, according to the Met Office, while large parts of England and all of Wales have already been officially declared in drought.The Environment Agency has warned that more areas of England could be declared in drought if dry conditions persist.Weather that was once considered extreme is becoming the "new normal", according to the latest Met Office report on the UK's climate.Its latest assessment found that the hottest day of the year in southern England is now 4.5C warmer than it was between 1961 and 1990."We are right now living in a time of historic and unprecedented change," said Mike Kendon, Met Office climate information scientist, adding that "evidence shows the climate of the 20th century has now gone".Scientists say El Niño may temporarily push global temperatures even higher. Its effects are being felt against a backdrop of man-made warming, particularly the burning of fossil fuels.The world is now about 1.4C warmer on average than it was in the late 19th Century.

schema.headline: World's oceans hit record-high July temperatures

title: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
description: Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on
body: Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way.But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life.Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving.Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges.There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted.The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate.We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond.Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks".We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death.It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder.In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting.One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers -  the case that Mathipa had been investigating.After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police.Outside the UK watch on YouTube, externalThe case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive.It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017.Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks. Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government.We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond.Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia.Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia.The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction.We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment.When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence.He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police.He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg.The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do.The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible.The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover.At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment.Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military.So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court.Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise.They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them.Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency.We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment.When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved.When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer."When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC.On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time.Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria.When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway.He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police.And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi.This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga's disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add.New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa's death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police's Criminal Intelligence division.Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, "we will kill all of them".Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa's special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo - both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case.The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction.All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody.Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa's murder, and Abotese's abduction and murder.

schema.headline: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC

title: How much parents could save from September's new school uniform rules
description: A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says
body: A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says will save them money.From September, uniforms will be limited to three items with a school logo, like a blazer, jumper or sportswear – plus a tie for secondary schools.Schools are already advised to keep these items to a minimum, meaning many are already within the rules, but about a quarter of schools will need to make changes by the time the law comes into effect.The government says the changes will save some families "up to £50 per child", but schoolwear suppliers say they now face uncertainty in demand for this year's uniforms.Co-op Academy Belle Vue, in Manchester, is planning to drop the number of its compulsory branded items from seven to three, plus a tie.It estimates the average cost of the branded parts of the uniform last year was £101.94 with a pinafore, and £83.95 without – but this year it will cost families an average of £53.97. Next year, when the school switches to a new supplier, it says it will fall further.The school has decided to get rid of its branded blazer, the branded pinafore, branded shorts and PE jogging bottoms. Because every school sets its own uniform policy, parents can still face very different expectations and costs.Lorraine, who lives in London, has two children in secondary schools and is frustrated that her school has not changed any of its uniform policy this year.She says several items are still compulsory, including the branded blazer, tie, branded polo shirt, branded shorts and two-toned PE socks.Even the plain grey trousers or skirt have to be purchased from one of the school's suppliers, she says.Both her sons have been through a growth spurt this summer, so she is expecting to spend more than £200 on their branded items alone."I'm just frustrated, for me it's not even about the money," she says."I feel these inconsistencies do not make a difference to education and are really blinkered."But mum-of-five Carol, from Stockport, welcomes the changes at her children's school. She says her son's secondary school only requires a branded blazer, a branded jumper and tie, with everything else available from a range of shops.She tries to get most of her children's uniforms second-hand anyway, but always buys the blazer, which costs around £30, as she likes them to have a new one.She says anything that makes it more affordable for parents is a good thing.But others are not seeing the changes they would like.One father from Oxfordshire, who did not want to be named, says his daughter still has to have seven branded items - three for the uniform, three for PE and a summer polo shirt - as there are no alternatives allowed. "It's ridiculous and unfair. We are paying £200 which we can't afford," he says.Most primary schools already have very few branded items.At Broadhurst Primary, in North Manchester, only the school jumper – and, from 2027, the PE T-shirt – are branded, which the school says brings the total cost of its uniform to £13 per child.Around 23% of secondary schools will have to change their uniform lists for September to comply with the new rules, according to the latest government survey.The education secretary has legal powers to direct schools to comply if they are not sticking to the new rules.One head teachers' union, the Association of School and College Leaders, says the actual difference in cost is likely to be marginal for most families.Its general secretary Pepe Di'Iasio says schools are already trying to balance the cost to parents with maintaining a sense of identity. He says it's also important to keep expensive fashion brands out so no one feels excluded.Some schools have been phasing their changes in over the last few years.King's Oak Academy, in Bristol, has one compulsory item left on its uniform list - a branded PE T-shirt.The school, which goes from reception right through to Year 11, used to have a branded jumper, tie and a shirt, which together cost about £41.Students are now asked to wear a plain polo shirt - which changes colour for the lower, middle and upper school - a sweatshirt or cardigan, and grey skirt or trousers, with all pupils also wearing black trainers. The school says it now costs about £10 to £25, depending on where parents buy the uniform.

schema.headline: How much parents could save from September's new school uniform rules

title: At least 13 killed in Ukrainian drone strike deep into Russia
description: At least 13 people have been killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, local officials have said. They confirmed one ch
body: At least 13 people have been killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, local officials have said. They confirmed one child was among those killed, with 75 more people injured as drones hit Nizhnekamsk, more than 1,100 kilometres (680m) from the Ukrainian border. Ukraine's Armed Forces said the city's Tanevo oil refinery had been hit.It is one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of Moscow's full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022. Kyiv has recently stepped up its long-range strikes on facilities it says contribute revenue and logistics to Russia's war on Ukraine.The strike on Nizhnekamsk lasted several hours overnight and into the morning, according to local sources. Verified images on social media show large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background. The Uzkbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan. According to Russian news agency RIA, most of the victims had been staying in a hostel at the time of the attack, and Russia's Investigative Committee said that "civilian individuals who were not involved in any military operations were present" where the drones struck. The BBC has not independently verified this information. Moscow said that "all those involved in the attacks" would "face inevitable and severe punishment".Oil refineries in Nizhnekamsk had already been hit once - on 12 June. "The facilities Ukraine targets are used to carry out attacks against Ukraine, manufacture weapons, support Russia's war effort," said Andriy Kovalenko, head of the Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation. The head of Tatarstan, Rustam Minnikhanov, confirmed the strike and shared his condolences with the families of the deceased, while Nizhnekamsk Mayor Radmir Belayev said the deaths had been a "a tremendous pain for all of us".Ukraine's Kovalenko said "every civilian death in Russia is on [President Vladimir] Putin" and that "Russians should direct their grievances at Putin and at the decisions made within their own country"."Without Putin, there would have been no aggression. Without the aggression, these people would still be alive," he added.More than 450 Ukrainian drones were shot down by the Russian air defences overnight across Russia, Moscow said. Elsewhere in Russia, fires broke out when an industrial facility in Siberia's Tyumen region was hit by several falling drones, according to local authorities.Kyiv has become increasingly successful at carrying out long-range strikes on Russia, often targeting warehouses or energy infrastructure, with civilian casualties mounting.Moscow, meanwhile, continues to target Ukraine with regular large-scale aerial attacks on cities and residential centres. Last week, a combined drone and missile strike on Kyiv killed 21 people.

schema.headline: At least 13 killed in Ukrainian drone strike deep into Russia

title: Thames Water gave finance chief a £1m signing-on fee
description: Thames Water paid its finance chief a £1m signing-on fee in July as the company struggles with a mountain of debt and faces temporary nationalisation.
body: Thames Water paid its finance chief a £1m signing-on fee in July as the company struggles with a mountain of debt and faces temporary nationalisation.Steve Buck joined the company in April 2025 but it is understood the seven-figure payment was not made until last month after the company had taken legal advice over its contractual obligations.The existence of the payment, first reported by Sky News,, external was revealed in a letter from the Thames Water chairman to MPs on the Commons Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee.In the letter,, external Sir Adrian Montague said he understood customers would see large payments to senior leaders as "unjust" but argued they were necessary to stop staff leaving.The letter said: "The majority of the team were brought in recently to fix the problems the company faces and are not responsible for causing those problems."These talented and experienced individuals have opportunities for roles outside Thames Water and, in many cases, have been actively approached by other companies. "These roles would be less in the public gaze, less difficult and more remunerative."Sir Adrian described the payment to Buck as a "necessary incentive" and said the money had come from emergency funding provided by Thames Water's lenders.He said the company is facing recruitment and retention difficulties and warned the problem would "persist" if it was nationalised or put into special administration. The prime minister's official spokesman said: "It's unacceptable that one of the worst-performing water companies is handing out huge payments to its executives when it should be focusing on improving performance and rebuilding public trust."We've banned bonuses for polluting water bosses. We expect companies to follow both the letter and the spirit of the rules."Under new rules, introduced last year, water companies failing to meet key standards would automatically lose their right to award certain bonuses. Alistair Carmichael, Lib Dem MP and chair of the Environment Committee, said: "Money should be going into improving services, not remunerating already well-paid senior executives."The government were clear in the early days that they wanted this to stop. It is obvious that they have not succeeded in this.  We need to hear now from them about what they intend to do about it."In a blog published in July,, external an executive director at the regulator Ofwat said public trust was damaged by unwarranted bonuses. Helen Campbell wrote: "This includes excessive payments made under the rationale of retaining leaders, but which are not transparent or sufficiently explained."She added that companies had to set out their reasoning for awarding particular bonuses and Ofwat would determine whether they had "complied with our rule".The utility company owes roughly £20bn and has been working with creditors and government officials to find a way forward.Failure to reach a deal could lead to Thames Water being forced into a "special administration regime", a form of temporary nationalisation intended to keep the business operating until a viable solution can be found.This would see government-appointed officials temporarily running the company – including funding its operations and upgrading infrastructure as well as dealing with any outstanding debts following a restructuring of the business.If the company was subsequently sold to a private buyer, the government would be able to recoup some taxpayer cash.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously said he would like to see "greater public control" of key water and energy utilities.In the past year, Thames Water boss Chris Weston saw his pay increase 14% to £1.63m while other directors received bonuses totalling £4.1m. Speaking on the BBC Big Boss interview late last month, Weston acknowledged there was anger about Thames Water pay, but argued that the company needed to be able attract "capable people to help turn this company around". "If we're not prepared to pay market rates, then they won't come to us and they won't stay with us," he said.Weston also warned special administration could see taxpayers left bearing the cost. Instead, he threw his weight behind a rescue deal that has been put forward by the firm's lenders. Thames Water has faced intense criticism for several years over failures to prevent sewage discharges and leaks.Last year it was handed a record fine of £122.7m from the regulator Ofwat, who said the company had "let down its customers and failed to protect the environment". Weston said he wanted the company to "do better" but some of the targets it had been set were "not realistic". Thames Water has warned it only has enough cash to last until the end of the year, putting pressure on the new government to decide what to do with the company, which provides water to 16 million people across London and the Thames Valley.Ministers could give the green light to the rescue deal, proposed by Thames Water's lenders, which would see some debts written off and new money invested in exchange for leniency on environmental targets.The previous Environment Secretary Emma Reynolds dismissed the plan as weak, arguing it did not do enough for consumers. She has since been replaced by Angela Eagle.

schema.headline: Thames Water gave finance chief a £1m signing-on fee
